terms.grammar: construction: the two demonstratives, each picking up one of two things just named
evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. hic: opposed to ille, “the latter … the former”
terms.comment: Latin has no word for “respectively”. English lists two sets and adds the word to pair them off (“Marcus and Julia are five and seven respectively”); Latin pairs them in the sentence itself. With two things, hic points to the nearer, the one named last, and ille to the farther, the one named first.
When the order does not matter, or each half gets its own clause: alter quīnque annōs nātus est, altera septem.
For “each to his own respective place, share or task”: suum cuique; in suam quisque domum.

phrases.latin: Mārcus quīnque annōs nātus est, Jūlia septem.
phrases.english: Marcus and Julia are five and seven respectively.
They went back to their respective homes.

no-word.html: An entry of a kind this lexicon keeps on purpose: where Latin has no equivalent, it says so and shows what Latin does instead.

sources: Lewis & Short: hic · Lewis & Short: alter · Lewis & Short: quisque
